articles.title: Deployment of AI Recruitment Tools in the EU: Employer Obligations Under GDPR and EU AI Act - ogletree.com
articles.summary: Deployment of AI Recruitment Tools in the EU: Employer Obligations Under GDPR and EU AI Act  ogletree.com
articles.full_text:
Quick Hits
- Spain’s data protection authority, the AEPD, issued a formal warning to a company before its AI recruitment tool was switched on.
- EU regulators demonstrate willingness to invoke their GDPR powers and intervene at the AI procurement stage.
- The EU AI Act lists as high-risk, under Annex III, certain types of AI recruitment tools including those that screen or filter applications, and evaluate candidates throughout the recruitment process.
- High-risk recruitment AI tools trigger human oversight and transparency obligations.
- Noncompliance with the GDPR can attract fines of up to €20 million or 4 percent of global annual turnover for employers.
- Noncompliance with the EU AI Act can attract fines of up to €35 million or 7 percent of global annual turnover for employers.
The AEPD recently issued a formal preventive warning to an organisation that was preparing to deploy an AI recruitment tool that would screen and evaluate job applications, and existing employee applications for internal mobility.
The AEPD acknowledged that AI can improve the efficiency and quality of hiring processes, although it stressed that data protection safeguards must be embedded from the very outset, reflecting the GDPR principle “data protection by design and by default.”
The AEPD highlighted several specific legal requirements when it comes to deploying an AI recruitment tool. Organisations must undertake a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) before the tool is used, where the processing is likely to result in a “high risk” to individuals’ rights and freedoms. Candidates and employees must receive clear and comprehensible information about how their personal data will be processed and the role the AI tool will play in evaluating them. Human oversight of outcomes is required by both the GDPR and the EU AI Act. This must be “effective,” meaning the decision-maker must be able to critically assess the score or output generated by the system and reach their own independent conclusion, rather than simply rubber-stamping the AI’s recommendation.
Practical Considerations
For employers wishing to deploy AI recruitment tools that will be used to rank and filter applications, the first step is to determine if the tool will be assisting recruitment decisions or influencing or determining decisions.
The GDPR (Article 22) gives individuals the right not to be subjected to decisions made solely through automated processing that would have a legal or similarly significant effect on them. The AEPD warning showcases how the functioning of an AI recruitment tool, and the level of human-intervention in the process outcomes, will be central to whether or not Article 22 applies.
If the tool will be influencing decisions, employers will need to undertake a DPIA, implement appropriate safeguards, notify individuals that automated decision-making is in use, update privacy notices describing the role of AI in the recruitment process, and ensure there is human oversight and documentation relating to this particular safeguard.
Additionally, the EU AI Act Annex III lists as high-risk AI recruitment tools that screen and filter candidates—this is the case even if the tool does not make the final recruitment decision. This classification means that employers will need to take compliance steps including:
- where applicable, performing a fundamental rights impact assessment;
- establishing a protocol for human oversight which would include the ability for someone to analyse, challenge, and override outcomes, maintain an in-depth understanding of how the AI works (e.g., how it is trained, tested, guardrails in place to minimise risk of bias, can verify and explain outcomes, has in place strong audit controls);
- documenting how the recruitment process relies on AI outcomes;
- providing training to their recruitment team; and
- updating privacy notices to inform individuals that they will be subject to automated decision-making.
Regulatory Action in the EU and the Impact on U.S. Employers
As governments and tech leaders discuss the regulation of AI the AEPD warning illustrates how EU regulators have already acted and are moving earlier and more assertively to enforce data protection and AI governance requirements around automated hiring technology, even before a tool goes live.
The AI recruitment tool in question is the type of cost-saving, efficiency tool that many employers are exploring and deploying. These tools will rapidly scan through applications, assign scores, and prioritise candidates. This strategically significant tech, with sizeable upfront costs, aims to reduce costly recruitment processes by speeding up the labor-intensive steps associated with resume review, and identify the best talent.
For U.S. employers that recruit candidates located in Europe, this is a reminder to build privacy and AI compliance into the recruitment tool procurement process before new recruitment tools are deployed. If the new recruitment tool is screening and filtering applications and candidates, then it is likely high-risk AI under the EU AI Act. If the new recruitment tool is capable of making decisions, rather than simply assisting the employer, it likely meets the automated decision-making threshold of the GDPR. Both legal frameworks impose strict requirements that must be complied with.

Simon J. McMenemy is the managing partner of Ogletree Deakins’ London office and co-chair of the firm’s Cybersecurity and Privacy Practice Group.
Nicola McCrudden is of counsel in the London office of Ogletree Deakins.

articles.title: How a Chinese ‘smart sex toys’ company fed Russian war tech against Ukraine — and exposed an EU sanctions blind spot - EUobserver
articles.summary: How a Chinese ‘smart sex toys’ company fed Russian war tech against Ukraine — and exposed an EU sanctions blind spot  EUobserver
articles.full_text:
“It takes years to sanction something that can be replicated in days—so what is the point of sanctions at all?”
This is a question we hear repeatedly in our work at the Independent Anti-Corruption Commission (NAKO) in Ukraine to close gaps in the sanctions regime.
And the frustration behind it is justified: several entities we submitted for designation years ago were added to the EU sanctions list only recently.
Since 2014, the European Union has sanctioned about 3,000 individuals and entities in relation to the war against Ukraine. The US has blacklisted over 7,000.
These lists include, among many others, third-country sanctions-evasion facilitators.
One such network exposed in late 2024 supplied microelectronics and British-made optical equipment later used in Russian military aircraft.
The UK sanctioned it nearly six months later; the EU took almost two years. It is one of hundreds, perhaps thousands, of such cases.
Sanctions take time: authorities must gather evidence, meet legal requirements, and assess their impact. Meanwhile, new companies can replace those under scrutiny, keeping the network running.
The British optics case shows how the main facilitator sourced goods from an alleged Hong Kong supplier of essential oils and confectionery flavourings — at an address shared with several companies already sanctioned for evasion.
(Almost) all roads lead to China
This essential-oils supplier was hardly an isolated curiosity.
It pointed to a wider infrastructure of shared addresses, corporate service providers, and unlikely businesses through which new suppliers can keep appearing as others are sanctioned.
Our study traced roughly 1,800 foreign suppliers and more than $800m [€702m] in trade in priority Western microelectronics—only a fraction of the true scale. Most passed through mainland China and, especially, Hong Kong.
China’s role in sanctions evasion — and the shell companies that help facilitate it — is hardly breaking news. But some suppliers in our dataset run very real businesses in rather unexpected fields.
Fuxin Pharmaceutical makes medicines and agrochemicals — and trades in Western microelectronics. Taibung Piping Equipment sells steel fittings for energy and petrochemical systems, alongside integrated circuits, semiconductors, and power electronics.
Shenzhen NuanQin Technology took things further.
It advertised “smart sex toys” but shipped to Russia no "Leopard Print Beginner’s Floggers" or "OMG! Feather Ticklers".
Customs records show industrial electronics, integrated circuits, and other dual-use components instead.
Its corporate footprint is equally eclectic: NuanQin is also linked to an FPV drone retailer.
Many others have generic names, no websites, and almost no public footprint.
To a Western dual-use manufacturer, they may look like small retailers or freight forwarders — unremarkable enough to pass conventional sanctions screening and keep trading.
Shared addresses are a red flag
Their addresses can reveal what company-by-company screening misses. Sharing one with a sanctioned firm does not warrant automatic designation, but it is a strong signal of diversion risk.
The numbers speak for themselves.
One Hong Kong office unit housed at least 45 companies, with perhaps 20 more: 14 under sanctions or export controls, and 31 unrestricted. Together, they supplied Russia with over $16m in priority microelectronics—within our dataset alone.
Other obscure suppliers lead businesses to claim they sell hats, salon equipment, or even offer immigration services.
Such links may be unsurprising in a world of virtual offices and corporate service providers, but a simple sanctions check misses them, even as tens of millions of dollars in trade pass through.
Beyond the shopfront
Offshore links recur throughout the data. We found 33 addresses associated with offshore structures and used by 66 suppliers, fewer than half of them restricted. Together, those suppliers accounted for over $57m in shipments to Russia, including $26m from unrestricted firms.
A shared office in the British Virgin Islands or Seychelles may raise an obvious red flag. Other connections are much harder to spot.
Take another Hong Kong supplier linked to millions of electronics and microelectronics supplies to Russia. Its ordinary-looking office address has also been used by offshore service providers and operators of tankers linked to Russia’s shadow fleet.
A shared address does not prove a coordinated network, but it points to corporate infrastructure serving both chip procurement and oil-sanctions evasion.
An even more striking case leads to Liu Baoxia. The United States sanctioned her in 2017, and the FBI placed her on its wanted list in 2025. Her network smuggled US electronics to Iran for its missile and drone programmes through Hong Kong front companies in the Ho King Commercial Center.
NAKO identified at least 14 companies supplying microelectronics to Russia from those same offices. Only five have been sanctioned.
Follow the address, not the company
Every company in our dataset, sanctioned or not, supplied Russia with priority microelectronics. We found more than 200 addresses linked to restricted entities. Over 450 suppliers used them, accounting for nearly $380m in trade.
Since 2024, the US Bureau of Industry and Security has listed high-risk addresses alongside company names.
Yet address-based screening remains limited, especially outside the United States. The Common High Priority List shows that governments can agree on shared diversion risks.
They should now do the same for addresses, particularly as Russian and Iranian procurement networks appear to use overlapping corporate infrastructure.
A shared list would help governments and manufacturers scrutinise replacement companies before each requires a separate investigation.
An address does not make every tenant guilty by association. But it should stop an ostensibly clean supplier from getting an automatic green light. Sanctions target companies; evasion networks reuse the infrastructure behind them.

articles.title: UK Considers Chinese EV Tariffs During EU Trade Discussions - Fuel Cells Works
articles.summary: UK Considers Chinese EV Tariffs During EU Trade Discussions  Fuel Cells Works
articles.full_text:
• The UK government is reviewing its tariff policy on Chinese electric vehicles as London seeks access to proposed “Made in Europe” measures amid reported EU pressure for closer alignment on Chinese EV tariffs.
• Britain does not impose the additional anti-subsidy duties introduced by the EU on Chinese-made EVs, while the UK automotive industry is warning that exclusion from “Made in Europe” measures could put an €80 billion [$94 billion] annual UK-EU automotive trading relationship at risk.
Britain is reviewing its tariff policy on Chinese electric vehicles as it seeks access for UK manufacturers to the European Union's proposed “Made in Europe” industrial measures.
UK Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said tariffs on Chinese EVs were “under review” and described the government's position as “finely balanced,” with different parts of Britain's automotive industry seeking different approaches.
“We are an export-orientated sector. So clearly, you shouldn’t do anything that risks your export markets, and you always have to take heed of retaliatory action if you put tariffs in place,” Reynolds told Politico at the Labour Party conference in Liverpool.
His comments come as London seeks to ensure British manufacturers are not excluded from the EU's proposed “Made in Europe” measures.
The Financial Times reported, citing people familiar with the discussions, that EU officials have pressed Britain to align more closely with the bloc's trade policy, including by raising tariffs on Chinese vehicles. The reported tariff linkage has not been publicly announced by the European Commission.
The UK did not follow the EU when Brussels imposed additional countervailing duties on battery-electric vehicles imported from China in 2024.
EU duties currently range from 7.8% to 35.3%, depending on the manufacturer, on top of the standard 10% import tariff. Britain has not introduced equivalent additional anti-subsidy duties on Chinese EVs.
The issue has become more prominent as Chinese brands increase their UK market share. Chinese-made vehicles account for around 16% of UK new-car sales this year, according to figures cited in reporting on the EU-UK discussions.
The discussions come as the EU works on its Industrial Accelerator Act and proposed “Made in Europe” provisions.
The legislation is intended to support European production through measures including public procurement and industrial support. Britain is concerned that UK-built vehicles and other products could fall outside parts of the framework.
Reynolds said excluding British industry would not serve the EU's objective of strengthening European manufacturing.
“The Made in Europe push is supposed to be about greater resilience, greater autonomy for European industry in the face of very significant pressures from both the U.S. and China,” Reynolds said. “Now, if that is the objective, it stands to reason that the U.K., that’s the second-biggest economy in Europe, should be a part of that.”
The Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders is also pressing for UK-built vehicles to be included.
Oxford Economics analysis commissioned by SMMT estimates that UK automotive production supports around €24 billion [$28 billion] of spending on EU-produced goods and services, 250,000 EU jobs and significant tax revenues.
The UK-EU automotive trading relationship is worth about €80 billion [$94 billion] annually, according to SMMT. Britain is the EU's largest export market for passenger cars, while the EU is Britain's largest passenger-car export market. The UK is also the largest importer of EU-built automotive components.
SMMT chief executive Mike Hawes said excluding British manufacturers from the proposed measures would reduce demand for EU-made components and affect manufacturers on both sides.
SMMT wants UK-produced vehicles to be treated as “assembled in the EU” for the purposes of the proposed rules.
The UK government has not committed to introducing additional tariffs on Chinese EVs.
Higher duties would bring British policy closer to the EU's approach but could expose UK exporters to Chinese retaliation and affect Britain's efforts to attract Chinese automotive investment.
Reynolds said those considerations are part of why the government regards the decision as finely balanced.

Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri held a series of meetings in New York on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), with discussions covering critical and emerging technologies, Pax Silica, semiconductors, critical minerals, energy security, civil nuclear cooperation.
                                    
            
        
                    
                    
                    
                                        Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri held a series of meetings in New York on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), with discussions covering critical and emerging technologies, Pax Silica, semiconductors, critical minerals, energy security, civil nuclear cooperation and the recently enacted Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act (SRIA).
In separate posts on X, Misri said he met US Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg and Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs Allison Hooker, with the engagements covering key areas of India-US bilateral cooperation.
"Great to meet Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg in New York. Agreed to advance India-U.S. cooperation in critical and emerging technologies, including through Pax Silica, and strengthen cooperation in semiconductors and critical minerals," Misri said.In another post, the Foreign Secretary said he discussed energy security and several other strategic issues with Hooker.
"A productive meeting with Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs Allison Hooker in New York today. Discussed various elements of India-US bilateral cooperation, including energy security and the recently enacted SRIA, civil nuclear cooperation, TRUST and the Indian Ocean Strategic Venture initiative," he said.
India-US cooperation in areas considered strategically important to economic and national security, including supply-chain resilience, advanced technologies and energy.
Pax Silica, launched in December 2025 by Helberg, is the US State Department's flagship initiative focused on AI and supply-chain security. The initiative seeks to build cooperation among partner countries around secure and innovative supply chains spanning critical minerals, energy inputs, advanced manufacturing, semiconductors and AI infrastructure.
The initiative has also expanded its membership. At the 2026 Summit, Argentina, Chile, Costa Rica, El Salvador, the European Union, Germany, Greece, Kazakhstan, the Netherlands and Panama joined the Pax Silica Declaration. The new additions brought the number of signatories to 24, alongside Australia, Finland, India, Israel, Japan, Norway, Qatar, South Korea, Singapore, Sweden, the Philippines, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom and the United States.
Taiwan has separately endorsed the declaration's principles through a joint statement on US-Taiwan economic security cooperation.The broader cooperation under Pax Silica has also included discussions on artificial intelligence and supply chain security. The United States and nearly three dozen Pax Silica economies signed a Joint Statement on AI Opportunity, with participants including India, Australia, Argentina, Germany, Japan, South Korea, the United Kingdom and the United States.
Against this backdrop, Misri's meeting with Helberg assumes significance for India's engagement with Washington on critical minerals and semiconductor supply chains, as both countries seek to deepen cooperation in strategic technologies and strengthen resilience in areas vulnerable to supply disruptions.
Misri's meeting with Hooker, meanwhile, covered energy security as well as the SRIA, civil nuclear cooperation, TRUST and the Indian Ocean Strategic Venture initiative.The discussion on SRIA comes as India continues to assess the implications of US legislation targeting Russia's energy trade and countries purchasing Russian oil and gas.
The Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, or SRIA, provides a statutory framework for expanded sanctions, import duties and trade restrictions concerning Russia, while also extending economic measures relating to Iran. The legislation focuses on areas including Russia's petroleum and military sectors, government officials, financial institutions and vessels associated with efforts to circumvent restrictions on Russian crude exports.
For India, the legislation has particular relevance because it creates a potential mechanism under which Washington could impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on imports from countries that continue purchasing Russian energy, subject to the statutory conditions and any subsequent invocation by the US President Donald Trump.The legislation itself, however, does not automatically impose a 100 per cent tariff on Indian goods. Rather, it provides the executive branch with authority to impose such tariffs under specified conditions.
India and China remain among the major purchasers of Russian crude, making the issue of continued energy trade with Moscow an important component of the wider discussion over sanctions and global energy markets.
New Delhi has maintained that its energy-security decisions are guided by national interests and market considerations. The Ministry of External Affairs has also said India is closely monitoring developments concerning the legislation and remains determined to protect its trade and economic interests.
With energy security featuring in Misri's discussions with Hooker and critical minerals, semiconductors and Pax Silica featuring in his engagement with Helberg, the meetings highlighted several of the major economic and strategic issues shaping the India-US relationship.
The engagements also come as India and the United States continue to work on cooperation spanning critical technologies, resilient supply chains, civil nuclear energy and strategic initiatives in the Indo-Pacific, alongside managing differences related to energy trade and sanctions policy.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Nato condemns Moscow’s ‘irresponsible nuclear rhetoric’ as strikes on Kyiv intensify - theguardian.com
articles.summary: Ukraine war briefing: Nato condemns Moscow’s ‘irresponsible nuclear rhetoric’ as strikes on Kyiv intensify  theguardian.comRussia’s tiny outpost in Europe could be Putin’s greatest weakness  The i PaperRussia Escalates Kaliningrad Rhetoric With Nuclear Threat Against NATO  UNITED24 MediaNATO Condemns ‘Nuclear Rhetoric’ in Tense Exchange With Russia  Bloomberg.comResidents of Polish region key for NATO try to live normally despite threat  The Japa...
articles.full_text:

  Nato on Tuesday condemned “irresponsible nuclear rhetoric” by Russia, after Moscow warned it would “deploy its entire arsenal” if the alliance threatens its exclave Kaliningrad. “I can confirm that Russia sent a non-paper to Nato and that we have sent a response, noting that Nato is a defensive Alliance and none of our activities or exercises pose a risk to any part of Russia,” Allison Hart, a Nato spokesperson, said. “We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric. We call on Russia to end its unprovoked war in Ukraine.”
- 
  Russia has intensified daytime strikes on Kyiv using jet-powered drones that Ukrainian forces are struggling to intercept. Russia fired ballistic missiles and dozens of jet-powered drones at Kyiv, Ukraine’s air force said Tuesday, as Moscow seeks to make Ukraine buckle under the pressure of day-and-night bombardment of its capital and other cities. Russia has used new jet-powered drones that fly too fast and too high for Ukrainian ground-based air defenses to shoot down.
- 
  Russia struck two datacentres in Kyiv overnight, a military-linked cargo vessel in the Black Sea, and another vessel with military cargo in the Ukrainian port of Odesa, the Russian defence ministry said on Tuesday. In a later evening statement, the ministry said its forces had launched a drone strike on a ship in the Black Sea which it said was carrying cargo intended for the Ukrainian armed forces.
- 
  Ukraine’s top university on Tuesday said it was ordering students to stay home as it switched to remote classes due to the surge in Russian daytime drone attacks on the capital. Kyiv’s Taras Shevchenko National University said it would “switch to a remote format of work” until at least 16 October, “due to the deteriorating security situation in Kyiv”. The university’s main campus is close to the National Academy of Sciences, which was hit by a drone strike, killing one person, on Monday.
- 
  Russian glide bombs struck a school in the northern Ukrainian city of Sumy on Tuesday, killing two people and injuring six, the regional governor said. The city’s governor, Oleh Hryhorov, said three children were among the injured. He said teachers and school officials had managed to evacuate 100 people.
- 
  Russia’s foreign investment envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, met US officials in Washington for talks about future US-Russia energy projects planned after Moscow’s war against Ukraine, a US government official told AFP. Dmitriev and US officials held “constructive discussions on a peaceful resolution to the Russia-Ukraine conflict and possible US-Russia energy initiatives after the war ends” on Monday, the official said on Tuesday. “The visit follows special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner’s recent meeting with president Putin in Moscow and their discussions last week with Ukrainian officials in NYC,” said the official, speaking anonymously.
- 
  The US president, Donald Trump, favours a proposal under which the US would lift some sanctions if Russia released a number of political prisoners, according to a report in the Atlantic. The White House did not comment directly on the report. When asked about the article, a US official told AFP that Trump was “committed to continuing to play a constructive role in ending the war between Russia and Ukraine, and he remains optimistic that we’ll ultimately get a peace deal done”.
- 
  Russia will cut funding for welfare, education and healthcare in next year’s state budget to help cover soaring military spending, fiscal documents obtained by Reuters showed. Russia plans to spend 17.1tn roubles (US$202.58bn) on defence in 2027, about 27% more than the 13.5tn roubles originally budgeted and the highest figure since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022. Funding for social policy, which covers items such as state pensions, payments to war veterans and maternity benefits, will shrink by 7%, while education funding will fall by 6% and healthcare by 6.8%.
- 
  Belgium will transfer three F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine by the end of the year to help in its war with Russia, Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said on Tuesday. Zelenskyy said Ukraine had already received “urgent deliveries” of F-16 ammunition from Belgium and Spain, among other countries. Zelenskyy later said later Ukraine had received a “very good” assistance package the day before of a NASAMS air defence system, developed jointly in the US and Norway.
- 
  A Russian nuclear-capable strategic bomber crashed Tuesday on a training mission in the country’s far east, killing six members of its crew, its defence ministry said. The ministry said in a statement that the Tu-95 bomber went down in an unpopulated area in the Amur region, adding that one crew member survived the crash and was hospitalised with injuries.

India reserves third-party rights in Russia-EU CBAM trade dispute in WTO
India has reserved its third-party rights in a WTO dispute filed by Russia against the European Union over its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, allowing New Delhi to follow the proceedings
Listen to This Article
India, along with several other countries, has reserved its third-party rights to participate in proceedings related to a trade dispute filed by Russia against the European Union over its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), as the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body has agreed to establish a panel to adjudicate the issue, an official said.
 
Argentina, Brazil, Canada, China, Chinese Taipei, Indonesia, Japan, Saudi Arabia, South Korea, Malaysia, Norway, Paraguay, Singapore, Switzerland, Thailand, the UK and the US are other countries that have reserved their third-party rights in the dispute, the Geneva-based official said.
 
Russia has filed a dispute against the EU's CBAM package and alleged export subsidy under the EU scheme for trading greenhouse gas emission allowances.
 
The WTO Dispute Settlement Body, at its meeting in Geneva on Friday, agreed to set up a panel to adjudicate the matter, the official said.
 
Another official said becoming a third party in the case will help India follow the proceedings in the dispute.
Also Read
"This is a constructive step for India as it will allow the country to see what is happening in the dispute. It can see the EU's as well as Russia's stand on the matter," the official added.
 
Third-party status would enable India to present its views on the WTO issues raised by Russia without becoming a principal party to the dispute.
The case is important for India because exporters of carbon-intensive products such as steel and aluminium face additional compliance requirements, including carbon costs and taxes, under the EU's CBAM regime.

articles.title: Rutte’s Germany Visit Comes as NATO Faces New Russian Threats Across Europe - finchannel
articles.summary: Rutte’s Germany Visit Comes as NATO Faces New Russian Threats Across Europe  finchannel
articles.full_text:
The FINANCIAL — NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte will travel to Münster, Germany, on October 1 for meetings with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten, as European intelligence agencies warn that Russia may intensify its campaign against NATO countries.
Rutte will also visit the 1st German-Netherlands Corps and deliver a speech at the 2026 International Westphalian Peace Prize ceremony. The visit comes less than three weeks after Rutte said Germany was playing a leading role in NATO’s military transformation and after NATO publicly backed Berlin following what Germany described as a Russian hybrid attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport.
On September 24, Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service said Russia was likely to intensify hybrid attacks against the West in coming months, with potentially greater consequences for targeted countries. It assessed a “low but growing risk” of a limited Russian military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia. The service said an outright invasion remained highly unlikely, although it could not be ruled out.
Days earlier, Czech intelligence chief Michal Koudelka told The Guardian that a limited Russian incursion, false-flag operation or major influence campaign could occur within “months, not years.” Baltic intelligence officials have taken a more cautious position, saying they see no evidence of an imminent attack.
NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, U.S. Air Force Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, said the alliance was increasing intelligence sharing in response to suspected Russian sabotage and other incidents.
Why Germany, France and Italy
Russia’s apparent strategy is lweakening the political and military coalition supporting Ukraine. Germany is particularly important because of its role in NATO logistics, military production and assistance to Ukraine. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has described the Leipzig incident as part of a broader pattern of Russian aggression against Europe.
Germany plans to spend €124.7 billion on defense-related military capabilities in 2026, equivalent to about 2.7% of GDP. The government expects military spending to reach at least 3.5% of GDP by 2029, with defense-related infrastructure adding another 1.5%.
France presents a different target. It is a nuclear-armed NATO member and one of Europe’s principal military powers. French authorities have documented Russian-linked information operations aimed at influencing political debate and undermining confidence in democratic institutions.
Italy is strategically important because of its Mediterranean position and role in NATO. In July, Italy expelled two Russian military attaches accused of espionage.
A September 24 report in Spain’s El Mundo, cited by ANSA, said U.S. intelligence had identified alleged Russian plans for drone attacks against France, Italy and Spain, potentially using drones launched from ships and concealed in containers. Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto said the alert had not been confirmed by Italian authorities. The report therefore remains an allegation rather than an established operational threat.
European intelligence assessments point to several potential Russian objectives: disrupting military assistance to Ukraine, forcing European governments to spend more on domestic security, creating political divisions and testing whether NATO members would respond collectively to a limited attack.
Recent events have given NATO a growing list of potential scenarios. Germany has blamed Russia for the Leipzig/Halle incident. Poland has investigated suspected sabotage affecting a Starlink facility supporting Ukrainian military communications. NATO has increased intelligence sharing in response.
The historical memory behind Europe’s response
Eastern Europe’s concern about Moscow also has a long historical foundation.
After World War II, the Soviet Union established political and military dominance across much of Central and Eastern Europe. Soviet forces crushed the Hungarian uprising in 1956 and led the Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968 after Alexander Dubček’s government introduced reforms.
The Soviet Union also occupied and incorporated Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania in 1940, an annexation the United States refused to recognize.
The Warsaw Pact, created in 1955, brought the Soviet Union together with Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Bulgaria, Romania, Albania and East Germany in a Soviet-led military alliance.
For the Baltic states and countries such as Poland, Russia’s current pressure is therefore viewed through a history in which Moscow previously used military force to maintain a sphere of influence in Eastern Europe.
Ukraine remains the center of the confrontation
Russia is conducting sustained missile and drone attacks against Ukraine while Ukraine has expanded strikes against Russian military and energy infrastructure. At the same time, European governments are increasing military spending and strengthening NATO’s eastern defenses.
Germany has permanently stationed a new armored brigade in Lithuania, while the 1st German-Netherlands Corps has taken a new command role on NATO’s eastern flank.
The result is a widening contest between Russia and NATO that increasingly extends beyond the battlefield.
For Rutte, Merz and Jetten, the October 1 meetings in Münster are likely to focus on how NATO can deter Russia, protect European infrastructure and maintain support for Ukraine while avoiding escalation into a direct NATO-Russia war.
RIA Novosti’s Deleted Lithuania Article Raises New Questions Over Russian Threats
A Russian state news agency briefly published an article on September 25 describing a potential conflict with NATO member Lithuania as another Russian “special military operation” and suggesting that Moscow could use nuclear-armed missiles. RIA Novosti deleted the article several hours later, saying it did not reflect the views of its editorial board, its editorial policy or Russian state policy.
The article, written by Alexander Nosovich, editor-in-chief of the Kaliningrad-based pro-Russian outlet RuBaltic.Ru, was titled “Russia Is In for Another SVO. It Will Be Very Short.” It appeared after Lithuania’s parliament advanced a proposal to remove the country’s constitutional prohibition on stationing nuclear weapons and foreign military bases.
Lithuania’s September 22 parliamentary vote was 99-13, with five abstentions. The vote did not itself authorize nuclear weapons or foreign bases in Lithuania; it advanced a constitutional change that would require further votes.
Nosovich argued that a conflict in the Baltic region would be much shorter than Russia’s war in Ukraine because of geography. He wrote that Russia could potentially avoid deploying ground forces and instead use missiles “with the appropriate warhead,” explicitly introducing a nuclear-strike scenario.
The article also used highly inflammatory language about Lithuania, describing it as a “suicidal country” and comparing it with Ukraine before Russia’s 2022 invasion.
On September 23, a Russian Mi-8 military helicopter crossed approximately 300 meters into Polish airspace near the Kaliningrad border and remained there for about 42 seconds, according to Polish authorities. Polish fighters were scrambled. Poland’s Operational Command said the circumstances could indicate that Russia was testing Polish air-defense readiness.
Earlier in September, NATO aircraft also shot down a drone that entered Lithuanian airspace. An Italian NATO fighter was involved, while a Russian warship separately fired two emergency flares near a Danish helicopter in the Baltic Sea.

articles.summary: France and Germany Push EU to Forge New Trade Tool Against China; Chinese Machinery Chamber Urges Brussels Not to Undermine Supply Chain Stability  finance.biggo.com
articles.full_text:
In response to reports that France and Germany are drafting a joint document urging the European Commission to strengthen its trade and economic security toolkit, the China Chamber of Commerce for Import and Export of Machinery and Electronic Products (CCCME) issued a statement on September 30 expressing "heightened concern" on behalf of China's machinery and electronics trade sector over the EU's protectionist tilt, and calling on Brussels to avoid negative legislation and policy implementation in order to jointly safeguard a fair and predictable bilateral trade environment.
A day earlier, a spokesperson for China's Ministry of Commerce had already responded to the matter in a press briefing, explicitly stating that the tool referenced in media reports "is a typical protectionist and unilateral measure," and warning that if the EU insists on introducing discriminatory restrictive measures, China will resolutely respond.
According to multiple media reports, France and Germany are pushing the European Commission to accelerate the development of a trade instrument widely dubbed a European version of the US "Section 301" tool, in order to adopt a tougher stance in economic and trade maneuvering with China. The so-called "Section 301" tool originates from Section 301 of the US Trade Act of 1974, which authorizes the US government to investigate foreign unfair trade practices and impose unilateral sanctions. If the EU follows suit, it would signal a further shift in its trade policy away from a rules-based multilateral framework toward unilateral pressure tactics.
In its statement, the CCCME noted that the Chinese and European economies are highly complementary, and that through long-term cooperation in machinery and electronics spanning goods trade, two-way investment and localized operations, technology R&D collaboration, and upstream-downstream coordination, the industrial chains of both sides have become deeply intertwined, with converging interests and mutual interdependence. The chamber emphasized that this industry ecosystem is the result of market forces and the independent choices of enterprises, having created substantial employment and development opportunities for both sides, and is worth cherishing and safeguarding.
The statement also pointed out that restrictive measures at both the legislative and administrative levels have been emerging with increasing frequency from the EU and its member states in recent periods, with a clear protectionist tendency that has caused deep concern among Chinese industry. Restrictive measures in trade and investment do not fundamentally enhance the EU's own industrial competitiveness; rather, they undermine mutually beneficial cooperation between enterprises and the stability and smooth functioning of supply chains, while also adversely affecting the interests of EU industry and consumers.
The CCCME said it has taken note of China's Ministry of Commerce's stern position against protectionist practices and its firm determination to safeguard China's economic and trade interests, and expressed full support for that stance.
The ministry spokesperson further elaborated on China's position in his response. He noted that the EU itself was once a victim of such unilateral tools, and that "one should not do unto others what one does not want done unto oneself." As an important member of the World Trade Organization, the EU has always portrayed itself as a champion of multilateralism. If it fails to lead by example and instead takes the lead in violating WTO rules, it would deal a severe blow to the rules-based multilateral trading system.
On the consultation process, the ministry spokesperson revealed that China and the EU are currently engaged in ongoing dialogue under their trade and investment consultation mechanism to explore ways to address each other's concerns. He warned that if the EU engages in dialogue and consultation with China on one hand while escalating pressure on the other, it would severely undermine mutual trust, disrupt the overall consultation process, and affect the broader picture of China-EU economic and trade cooperation.
The CCCME concluded its statement by urging the EU to seriously heed the voice of industry and to resolve differences through intergovernmental consultations and industry dialogue. The chamber said it will closely monitor relevant developments, assist machinery and electronics enterprises in properly responding to external risks and challenges, and strive to play a positive role in safeguarding the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese industry and the broader China-EU economic and trade relationship.
From a timeline perspective, the situation is evolving rapidly. The Franco-German joint document is still in the drafting stage, and whether the European Commission will adopt it—and in what form it might be implemented—remains uncertain. However, China's response has already sent clear signals simultaneously from both the government and industry levels: on one hand, expressing opposition through diplomatic channels while reserving countermeasure options; on the other, conveying the deep concerns of industry through trade associations.
China-EU machinery and electronics trade occupies a pivotal position in bilateral economic relations. Chinese machinery and electronic products—spanning mechanical equipment, electronic products, auto parts, home appliances, and other broad categories—have for years been the mainstay of China's exports to Europe. At the same time, European companies' investments in manufacturing facilities in China, technology cooperation, and supply chain arrangements are highly dependent on the Chinese market's manufacturing capacity and consumption potential. If the EU rashly introduces new restrictive tools, the first to bear the brunt would be not only Chinese exporters but also a large number of European manufacturers operating in China and their downstream customers back home.
Analysts note that the internal dynamics of EU trade policy toward China are becoming increasingly complex. France and Germany, as the EU's two core economies, are moving in lockstep on strengthening trade defense tools, reflecting Europe's collective anxiety in the face of China's rising industrial competitiveness. At the same time, divergences of interest among EU member states persist—industries and regions highly dependent on exports to China are clearly less able to withstand an escalation in trade frictions.
China's response deliberately emphasized the existing channels of "dialogue" and "consultation," signaling an intention to leave room for de-escalation. The ministry spokesperson's phrasing that China will "closely monitor the EU's subsequent actions" has been interpreted by observers as indicating that Beijing will calibrate the intensity of its countermeasures based on the EU's actual moves rather than media reports, reflecting strategic prudence and flexibility.

Monetary Policy And Market Positioning

This mismatch means broader inflation figures could remain stubborn, forcing policymakers to keep interest rates elevated for longer than the market previously priced.

Energy Sector Strategies And Volatility Hedges
In the energy sector, we should focus on the widening gap between raw crude and refined fuels by trading the diesel crack spread. Buying European Gasoil futures while simultaneously shorting Brent crude allows us to capture the structural premium on refined products. Historical data shows that refining bottlenecks keep diesel prices elevated even when raw oil supply increases, a trend that is currently intensifying across European hubs.
Implied volatility in Eurozone interest rate options remains relatively low, creating cheap entry points for protective strategies. We suggest buying payer swaptions to hedge against sudden spikes in European bond yields over the next month. This setup protects portfolios against a sharp sell-off in fixed income if upcoming inflation data prints hotter than expected.

articles.title: Latvia’s Election: Rail Baltica Is a NATO Problem, Not a Budget Scandal - moderndiplomacy.eu
articles.summary: Latvia’s Election: Rail Baltica Is a NATO Problem, Not a Budget Scandal  moderndiplomacy.eu
articles.full_text:
Eurofighters Over Lielvārde
This week, four German Eurofighters and several dozen ground crew arrived at Lielvārde air base in central Latvia. They were sent at Riga’s request to protect the country’s airspace through Saturday’s election. The deployment follows a spring in which drones repeatedly crashed on Latvian territory. They were mostly Ukrainian drones aimed at Russian oil ports and pushed off course by Russian jamming. One exploded at an oil depot in Rēzekne, 40 km from the Russian border, and the defence minister resigned.
On the ground, however, the campaign has been about something else. According to OSW, the Polish think tank, it has centred on the finances of the national airline airBaltic, delays to the Rail Baltica railway and state funding for NGOs. The jets are protecting a vote that has barely mentioned them.
A Frontline Election About Everything Else
Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs took office in May, ending a series of coalition crises, and his United List has led the polls since. The Robert Schuman Foundation’s summary of early-September polling has the United List at 23.6%, Latvia First at 12.6%, the National Alliance at 11%, the Progressives at 10.7%, the Union of Greens and Farmers at 10.4%, the Sovereign Power alliance at 9.6% and New Unity at 8.9%. Seven parties look set to pass the 5% threshold. The expected result is a coalition of Latvian parties led by Kulbergs. Its main shared purpose is to keep out the two parties that draw most heavily on Russian-speaking voters: Ainārs Šlesers’s Latvia First and Sovereign Power.
Latvia plans to spend about 4.9% of GDP on defence, among the highest shares in NATO. No major Latvian party campaigns against that figure. That consensus is why defence barely features in the debate.
The Railway Is the Reinforcement Plan
The usual reading is that Latvians have moved on to everyday concerns. The better reading is that the consensus on defence has hidden the one security issue the country does argue about, Rail Baltica, by treating it as a question of cost overruns.
Rail Baltica is an 870-km standard-gauge line from Tallinn to the Lithuanian–Polish border. The Baltic states still run on the 1,520 mm Russian gauge, which forces every NATO train arriving from Poland to stop and transfer its load. Railways are the best way to move armoured vehicles and heavy equipment to the Baltics, and Rail Baltica was designed from the start to carry troops and heavy military equipment from west to east. In May, NATO assigned the German-Netherlands Corps to Latvia and Estonia, a command intended to receive 40,000 to 60,000 soldiers in a crisis. That plan assumes those troops and their equipment can get there. Without a continuous standard-gauge line, reinforcements depend on roads, ports and slow transfers between gauges.
This is where the budget debate misses the security question. The European Court of Auditors puts the whole project at €23.8 billion, up from €5.8 billion in 2017. The first phase, a single track, needs about €15 billion, with only about €5 billion secured. Latvia’s share of the overrun is around €5.5 billion. The chief executive of RB Rail, the joint venture running the project, says “saving money will almost certainly mean losing time.” Latvia is widely seen as the section most likely to fall behind.
The man most likely to lead the next government has already said what that means. As chair of the Saeima’s Rail Baltica inquiry in May 2025, Kulbergs said it would take “at least seven to eight years” to reach Salaspils, making 2035 the earliest date to reach the Estonian border. As Prime Minister in June, he rejected fixed deadlines, arguing that “a deadline of the 30th or any fixed date has the opposite effect. It creates stress.” As a budget position, that is defensible. As a defence position, it means Latvia is planning for Estonia’s reinforcement route to have a gap through the middle of the country for five years longer than NATO’s plans assume.
The second overlooked issue is the fifth of voters the coalition is designed to exclude. Russian speakers make up about a quarter of Latvia’s population. Latvia First and Sovereign Power together poll around 20 to 22%. The mainstream parties see both as outside Latvia’s security consensus, and Russia does use the Russian-speaking minority as a political lever. Moscow’s envoy at the UN has already threatened the Baltic states with retaliation, despite their NATO membership. But governing permanently without a fifth of the electorate has costs during a hybrid campaign. New rules restricting Russian in schools and the media, and a large group of long-term “non-citizens,” give Russian information operations material to work with. Excluding these parties is a legitimate choice. Doing it without offering those voters anything is where the risk lies.
The strongest objection is that Rail Baltica is a slow, peacetime project that no wartime plan relies on, and that NATO will reinforce the Baltics by air, sea and road whatever happens to it. That is true for the first days of a crisis. It is not true for the following weeks, when tanks, artillery and ammunition have to move in bulk, which is exactly the load railways carry and roads handle poorly. A reinforcement plan built around a railway that stops at the Latvian border does not fully work.
Three Coalitions, Three Railways
Base case (around 55%): a Kulbergs coalition with a vague Rail Baltica commitment. The United List forms a government with the National Alliance and the Greens and Farmers, possibly adding New Unity or the Progressives. The coalition agreement confirms Rail Baltica in general terms but sets no national funding share and no binding deadline. Latvia waits for the EU’s post-2028 budget. The combined vote of Latvia First and Sovereign Power lands around 20 to 25%. Their voters remain outside government, and the parties become the main opposition. The key assumption is that no drone incident or security shock during the coalition talks forces defence back to the top of the agenda.
Downside (around 25%): a weak coalition and a railway that drifts. A fragmented result forces a coalition of four or five parties that is already arguing over airBaltic and the budget. Rail Baltica funding slips another year, and Estonia begins domestic services on its own section, leaving Latvia as the obvious gap in the line. If the Russian-speaking parties do well above 25%, Moscow will present the result as proof of discrimination. For readers, the exposure falls on Baltic construction and logistics contracts, and on NATO planners who have assumed rail capacity will exist.
Upside (around 20%): Rail Baltica is funded as defence spending. The new government, pressed by NATO and Brussels, reclassifies part of Latvia’s share of Rail Baltica as military mobility spending that counts towards the 5% NATO target. That unlocks national money and possibly EU defence funds. This alone would turn the project from a budget scandal into a defence programme.
The Line on the Map
Latvia’s election is not a sign that security matters less on NATO’s frontline. It shows that defence is so settled that the one strategic issue voters still argue about, the railway meant to bring NATO troops into the country, is debated in the language of cost overruns. Meanwhile, a coalition built to exclude a fifth of voters will govern during a hybrid campaign aimed at exactly those voters.
Watch for two numbers after Saturday. The first is the combined vote share of Latvia First and Sovereign Power. The second is the Rail Baltica wording in the coalition agreement: a national funding share and a completion date would mean the new government treats it as defence. Vague language would mean the gap in the line continues.
NATO has sent jets to protect Latvia’s vote. What reinforcement actually depends on is a railway that the likely next Prime Minister does not want tied to a deadline.

articles.title: ‘All-in' Russia invasion warning as NATO's two major weaknesses exposed - AOL.co.uk
articles.summary: ‘All-in' Russia invasion warning as NATO's two major weaknesses exposed  AOL.co.uk
articles.full_text:
Russia would have to go "all-in" if it were to launch an incursion into Estonia, an expert has said. There has been speculation over recent days at to whether the Kremlin could orchestrate a takeover of part of the Baltic country. The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) suggested that Russian agents would take over major buildings in Narva. Experts also pointed out that long-range drones could be launched from Russia.
Merili Arjakas, a research fellow at The International Centre for Defence and Security (ICDS) - a think tank in Estonia specialising in security, defence and foreign policy issues - and the editor-in-chief of foreign policy magazine Diplomaatia, told The Express: "Russia cannot expect that any such attack against Estonia or the Baltic states will remain limited, as if the European states had not learned anything from the annexation in Crimea and the war in Donbas, which led to the full-scale invasion eight years later.
"That is not to say that Russia is not an aggressive power or that Putin does not dream of the collapse of NATO. Rather, any incursion will face a strong and immediate response from us and our partners."
A small-scale operation would not be sufficient, Ms Arjakas suggested.
She said: "Therefore, if I were Russia and I wanted to attack Estonia or the Baltics, I would go all-in, not think that any limited incursion to Narva or to other places would be enough.
"Fortunately for us, Russia has so far been careful to not create conditions for a large-scale confrontation with NATO. Its tolerance of such risk has certainly increased as they carry out more attacks that fall below the threshold for triggering Article 5.
"However, such asymmetric escalation is also characteristic of a weaker party, one that still deems it too risky to use conventional means."
Estonia is "taking the threat seriously", the specialist added, while also pointing major NATO weaknesses.
"Our defence budget for 2026 is 5.4% of GDP (€2.4billion), with major spending on ammunition, medium-range air defence, HIMARS, UAVs, anti-tank systems and territorial defence," Ms Arjakas said.
"Similar investments have been done by Latvia, Lithuania, and Poland, while Finland has long been a shining example of a country armed to the teeth and prepared to fight.
"There are vulnerabilities - particularly in defence against missiles and drones, as well as in terms of reinforcement and logistics in the event of a full-scale invasion. But these are not vulnerabilities unique to Estonia or the eastern flank; rather, they are shared by all NATO countries except the US.
"Our best way of avoiding a NATO-Russia war, whether it erupts here or elsewhere, is still to support Ukraine so the aggressor does not prevail there. Ukraine keeps Russian forces and resources tied down and degrades Russian military capacity, thereby not only fighting for its own survival and sovereignty but also acting as a shield for Europe."

Updates to Russia/Belarus sanctions from EU and UK (and major US developments)
With the rapid expansion of UK, EU and US sanctions on Russia and Belarus in recent weeks - and with more in the regulatory pipeline - we set out:
If you would like to discuss any sanctions-related issues with a specialist, please contact Partner Andrew Hood, who would be pleased to arrange an initial conversation about your query: Andrew.Hood@fieldfisher.com or +44 330 460 6968.
1. WHAT'S NEW
Key sanctions developments from the UK, EU and US from September 2026.
i. UK
- On 14 September 2026, the Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation (OFSI) added FAQ 203 on crediting interest to frozen accounts of designated persons. FAQ 203 clarifies that interest may be credited only to the frozen account in which it accrues, and not to another frozen account even if it is held by the same designated person. OFSI reminds firms to consider whether a licence is required before making such payments.
ii. EU
- On 21 September 2026, European Commission Vice President, Kaja Kallas, confirmed that the EU will impose new sanctions on those involved in organising the Russian State Duma elections held between 18 – 20 September 2026. Her statement notes that "those involved in organising these sham elections or standing as candidates in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, as well as those responsible for undermining the possibility of free and fair elections inside Russia, will be sanctioned". Further details of the proposed sanctions have not yet been announced.
- On 16 September 2026, European Commission President, Ursula von der Leyen, made her State of the Union speech sharing her key priorities and strategic direction for the year to come. In relation to Russia sanctions, von der Leyen stated that "the pressure on Russia must continue to increase…and this does not always require new sanctions, but above all the enforcement of existing ones". The speech made no indication of when the European Commission is set to deliver the 22nd EU sanctions package.
- On 14 September 2026, the EU failed to extend its asset freeze regulation following a demand from Slovakia that the EU remove Alisher Usmanov and Michail Fridman from the list. France has reportedly attempted to create a compromise by suggesting that Alisher Usmanov be delisted. Member States agreed on a one-week extension to allow negotiations to continue on the six-monthly rollover of the sanctions, which requires the unanimous approval of the 27 Member States.
- On 12 September 2026, Advocate General Medina (the "AG") issued a non-binding opinion on the scope of Article 5k of Regulation (EU) 833/2014. The AG's view is that the Article 5k prohibition on certain Russian nationals and companies being awarded public procurement contracts only applies where a contract is in scope of the EU public procurement framework, including the EU's threshold amounts. Member States cannot expand the scope of the Article even if their domestic legislation applies procurement rules to lower-value contracts.
iii. US
- On 16 September 2026, the United States House passed the H.R.5334 Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. For more detail, please refer to: The New US Sanctioning Russia Act: Considerations for Businesses. 
2. YOUR 5-STEP CHECKLIST
Working through the following 5 questions will help you to better manage your business's sanctions compliance:
We step through the key considerations that will help you answer each question below.
- Which countries’ sanctions apply to your activities?
The UK, EU, US and other countries’ sanctions typically must be observed if there is a sufficient nexus to confer jurisdiction, that is if:
- their nationals (individuals) are involved, wherever they are in the world (in the case of US sanctions, this includes US permanent residents/Green Card holders);
- any part of a transaction is conducted within their territory or airspace; and
- legal entities incorporated or constituted under their law, including foreign branches are involved; or
- with respect to US sanctions, if a transaction is conducted in US dollars or clears through the US financial system, or data is routed through servers in the US, or other back-office support or facilitation is provided by US persons (including service requests to an equipment supplier). Non-US persons may be penalised if they cause US persons to violate US sanctions, for example omitting reference to the involvement of a sanctioned party or jurisdiction to a financial transaction involving a US person.
UK sanctions may also apply to non-UK persons outside the UK if there is a sufficient nexus. This will depend on the facts of each case but could include:
- transactions using clearing services in the UK;
- actions by a local subsidiary of a UK company;
- actions directed from within the UK; and/or
- financial products or insurance bought on UK markets but held or used overseas.
Additionally, US ‘secondary sanctions’ may be applied to non-US persons outside the US in the absence of any US nexus if a transaction involves sanctionable conduct that would be prohibited to a US person and that is determined by the US authorities to be a ‘significant’ transaction or otherwise provides material support to a sanctioned party. Whether a transaction is ‘significant’ is based on a number of open-ended criteria e.g. the size, number and frequency of transactions.
Further, US export control restrictions may apply even if sanctions do not. For example, US export controls will apply if US-origin goods, software or technology located in a third country are re-exported, regardless of whether a U.S. person is involved in the transaction.
- Are any of your business partners (banks, suppliers, customers, distributors etc.) subject to an asset freeze?
The UK, EU, US and others have imposed asset freezes (‘blocking sanctions’ in US terms) on most Russian banks, individuals and entities involved in strategic industries (e.g. defence, energy, finance, transport, research, media and aerospace), and senior individuals in the Russian government, state-owned corporations and major businesses, including family members, and they are continuing to add new names to their national lists of such ‘designated persons’. As the various sanctions regimes have matured, asset freezes have increasingly been imposed on third country entities and individuals (including those based in China, Turkey, the UAE etc.).
An asset freeze generally requires those within the scope of the national sanctions, as described at step 1 (above), to:
- freeze any assets of the designated parties that they may hold and to report these to their authorities;
- not make any funds or economic resources available to them, directly, indirectly or for their benefit (economic resources are broadly defined).
US and some EU restrictions go further and prohibit all transactions with the designated (i.e. listed) party.
The same restrictions also apply to any non-designated entity that is:
- ‘owned’ by a designated party or parties. The US and EU threshold is 50% or more, while the UK threshold is ‘more than 50%’. The US and the EU (in guidance) consider the criterion met if the aggregated ownership of two or more designated parties exceeds the threshold. The UK recognises aggregated ownership only if there is evidence of a joint arrangement between two or more designated parties; or
- (in the UK/EU, not the US) ‘controlled’ by a designated entity (i.e. able to ensure the affairs of the undesignated entity are conducted in accordance with their wishes, for example through controlling a majority of voting shares or having the right to appoint or remove a majority of the board of directors).
'Control' considerations:
It is often challenging to reach a definitive view of whether this ‘control’ criterion is applicable, for example if a majority shareholder becomes sanctioned and passes some of their shares to unsanctioned family members or to business associates. Some key considerations are set out below:
UK: The UK courts and Government have all contributed to a somewhat uncertain definition of 'control'.
The Court of Appeal's 2023 judgment in Boris Mints & Ors v PJSC National Bank Trust (NBT) & Anor implies that all Russian state-owned companies may be controlled by President Putin, a designated person. The judgement is being appealed to the Supreme Court.
The UK High Court's judgment in Hellard v OJSC Rossiysky Kredit Bank & Ors discusses the test for "control" in light of the Mints judgment, breaking the concept of control into 4 categories: de jure control; actual present de facto control; potential future de jure control and potential future de facto control.
UK Government guidance published after the ruling in Mints states that: "If [Government] considered that a public official was exercising control over the public body under UK sanctions regulations, [the Government] would look to designate the public body where possible when designating the relevant public official." That is, in the view of the UK Government, simply being run or overseen by a UK designated public official would not of itself mean the organisation is subject to UK sanctions.
The 2025 High Court judgment in Nikolay Fetisov & Ilya Yurov & PJSC National Bank Trust applied the above judgments when considering whether President Putin and/or Central Bank of the Russian Federation Governor Elvira Nabiullina "control" NBT (the same entity considered in the Mints decision. In this case, the Court found that the absence of evidence of potential de facto control was significant, ultimately deciding that NBT was not "controlled" by a designated person and therefore did not need to be treated as subject to an asset freeze. This aligned with a statement from OFSI presented in evidence noting that "OFSI does not consider NBT to be subject to sanctions."

articles.full_text:
Good morning. A scoop to start: Belgium has warned that the US under Donald Trump is no longer a reliable ally and urged its diplomats to cultivate ties with his opponents to protect the country’s interests, according to an internal document seen by the FT.
Today, our industry correspondents report on the tussle over defining “Made in Europe”, and the EU’s defence commissioner criticises the decision to lift sanctions on two Russian oligarchs.
Drawing a line
Industry ministers descend on Brussels for heated discussions on the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) today, with France and Germany at odds over what “Made in Europe” should really mean, write Ian Johnston and Barbara Moens.
Context: Defining “Made in Europe” has serious consequences for the automotive and cleantech sectors impacted by the IAA. It will also influence future legislation as the EU develops a more muscular industrial policy that spells an end to years of free-trade ideology.
The IAA proposes to give a European preference to subsidies and public contracts in sectors such as electric vehicles and batteries. EU capitals disagree over whether to also include manufacturers from free-trade partners such as the UK, Canada and Japan. One senior diplomat said that there had been a “huge amount of interest in the geographic scope”.
Diplomats are not set to formally tackle the issue until October 7 but today’s discussions will allow ministers to set the political tone. French industry minister Sébastien Martin told journalists on Tuesday that “the EU is the EU27. That’s the starting point”.
But a recent German position paper seen by the FT supports a “made with EU” approach: free-trade partners or those in a customs union (read: Turkey) are “in principle to be treated as equivalent to ‘Union origin’”.
Some member states are concerned that too broad a definition of “Europe” could lead to circumvention. For example, Chinese companies investing in Turkey would negate the IAA’s aims to boost European manufacturing, diplomats said.
Germany, by contrast, argues it is “not in our economic interest to close markets to one another”.
Meanwhile, Spain is preparing a new proposal to break the deadlock, several diplomats said, which could help define which trade partners are included.
But Germany and France are also discussing the phaseout of combustion engines by 2035, with France ready to be “flexible” if there is a “real Made in Europe”, Martin said.
Poland’s deputy industry minister Michał Baranowski told the FT that he supported a “balanced approach” that “recognises our important links with trade partners. I think that’s ultimately where we will end up.”
Industry ministers will also discuss the bloc’s Chips Act 2.0, which aims to strengthen Europe’s semiconductor industry and reduce strategic dependencies.
According to a preparatory document seen by the FT, Ireland as chair of the discussions wants a political steer from European capitals on how to “best balance technological sovereignty, economic competitiveness and international co-operation in developing its semiconductor ecosystem”.
Chart du jour: ‘Into the fire’
A radical proposal by the French far left to “cancel” a chunk of the country’s debt has become a prominent issue in the country’s nascent presidential race.
Warning signals
The shock lifting of sanctions on two Russian oligarchs is “not a good signal”, the EU’s defence commissioner told Andy Bounds, adding to a chorus of disapproval.
Context: EU ambassadors this week lifted curbs on Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, prompting fears that the sanctions regime was fracturing.
“I consider that really not the best decision,” Andrius Kubilius said, adding that there was some comfort in another change, which means sanctions will now be renewed every three years rather than every six months.
France demanded Usmanov’s delisting as part of a secret prisoner release deal involving Azerbaijan. A French citizen accused of spying was duly pardoned yesterday. Luxembourg championed Fridman, who has a $16bn damages case against the Grand Duchy.
The billionaires are the richest Russians to be cut from the list and follow the watering down of gas sanctions in July to please Greece.
Kubilius, a Lithuanian, rejected concerns about war fatigue in some member states, but conceded there was concern that Russian hybrid attacks were influencing some people in Poland and other countries neighbouring Ukraine to question the cost of supporting Kyiv.
He said that there was a need for “a serious discussion on our strategy for how we end this war . . . peace through strength by strengthening Ukraine”.
Kubilius said the sanctions developments should give fresh impetus to a campaign by some countries to replace the need for unanimity in foreign policy decisions including sanctions with qualified majority voting.
He said European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen had made the point in her State of the Union speech last week: “Our doctrines, institutions and decision-making, especially in this area of foreign policy and security policy, were created during peacetime and now they are not fit for the changing circumstances.”
What to watch today
- EU competitiveness ministers meet.
- Leaders of Cyprus, Finland, Croatia and Greece attend the Europe Gulf Forum in New York.
Now read these

- Kremlin money laundering: State-owned oil group Rosneft was at the heart of Russia’s efforts to circumvent sanctions, an FT investigation shows.
- Exposed: France, Germany and the UK are disproportionately exposed to potential economic coercion by Beijing.
