- list 3 of 3Russian strikes kill eight, injure dozens across Ukraine
The attacks come as Russia has begun hitting Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities with faster, high-flying jet drones.
Emergency officials said the strike on the National Academy of Sciences on Monday killed two people, with one person’s body recovered from the rubble later in the evening.
Video shared online appeared to show a fast-moving drone slamming into the building at a steep angle and exploding, sending smoke into a clear sky. People were seen leaning out of windows as bright orange flames engulfed part of the building.
Volodymyr Horbulin, a former secretary of Ukraine’s National Security and Defence Council, told the public broadcaster Suspilne that he was at work at the academy when it came under attack. He said his assistant, who was near the building, was killed and that he was also slightly wounded.
The academy is near the German Embassy, a cathedral, the national opera and government buildings.
In a statement, the academy called the attack “Russian terror” and “barbarity” aimed at “peaceful people who were simply at their workplaces”.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha accused Russia of cynicism for hitting a scientific institution during the workday.
“Russia is deliberately expanding the boundaries of what it believes the world will tolerate,” he said in a statement, urging Ukraine’s allies to provide more air defences.
Jet-powered drones
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russian forces also hit a medical facility in Kyiv on Monday. He said at least nine people had been killed in Russian drone strikes throughout the country, while more than 80 people were wounded.
In his nightly video address, Zelenskyy said Ukraine was still having difficulty countering the faster, high-flying Russian jet-powered drones.
“New interceptors are being actively tested,” he said. “Some combat groups are using them, but, of course, some details still need to be refined to achieve enough effectiveness and scale. We are speeding up the developers.”
According to the Ukrainian president, 90 of 120 drones fired on Ukraine on Monday were jet-propelled, rather than propeller-driven, with an interception rate for this type of drone at 57 percent.
Widening targets
Officials said the Russian strikes on Kyiv also targeted a pharmaceutical company and petrol stations. In other cities and regions, civilian facilities, businesses and communications infrastructure were hit.
In the southeastern city of Dnipro, a Russian drone attack on a business centre killed three people and wounded 19, according to officials. Another person was killed in a logistics office in Synelnykove, southeast of Dnipro, the regional governor said.
Emergency services said an attack on infrastructure in the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia wounded 32 people.
Al Jazeera’s Jonah Hull, reporting from Kyiv, said Russia has been hitting economic targets across Ukraine “in a rolling series of strikes that have been ongoing for six days now”, during the day and night.
“Data centres increasingly being hit, as well as digital and communications infrastructure,” he said. “Kyiv Star, the country’s biggest cell provider, was hit on Sunday, as was the second biggest, Vodafone Ukraine. The government is said to be preparing for the worst: a total blackout in communications should that come.”
The Russian attacks have brought Kyiv “firmly into the eye of this war”, Hull added.
Ukraine has also increased attacks on Russia, targeting oil refineries as well as online retailers to try to undermine revenues and support for Moscow’s war effort.
Zelenskyy said on Monday that Ukraine struck Russian oil facilities in the Krasnodar region and two defence plants.
Both sides have denied deliberately targeting civilians.

articles.title: The Mathematical Myth Of '100% Renewables': Why The Green Transition Requires A Nuclear Renaissance - OpEd - Eurasia Review
articles.summary: The Mathematical Myth Of '100% Renewables': Why The Green Transition Requires A Nuclear Renaissance - OpEd  Eurasia Review
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways:
- The author calls 100% wind-and-solar climate policy an “illusion”: industrial grids need unwavering baseload, weather does not supply it, and multi-day Dunkelflaute storage would demand battery and mineral scale he says is economically and geopolitically unreal—trading an atmospheric problem for a mining one.
- Germany’s Energiewende is the case study: huge spend on wind and solar, early nuclear shutdowns, among the world’s highest industrial power prices, and lignite when the wind drops. AI data centers that run 24/7, he argues, make low-EROI intermittent-plus-battery grids even less viable.
- The prescribed fix is a nuclear renaissance, especially SMRs: dense, dispatchable, small-footprint, able to use existing grid connections for industry, desalination, and the digital economy. Nations that skip firm clean power, he says, get instability, high prices, and industrial flight.
For over a decade, a comforting illusion has dominated global climate policy: the belief that the modern economy can operate entirely on wind and solar power. It is an appealing narrative, heavily marketed by environmental lobbies and enthusiastically adopted by politicians seeking rapid green credentials. However, when this “100% renewable” utopia is subjected to the cold, unforgiving arithmetic of energy economics and grid engineering, the narrative rapidly collapses.
The foundational flaw in the purely renewable model is the physics of intermittency. Modern industrial economies demand a constant, unwavering supply of electricity—the baseload. Wind and solar are inherently erratic. They do not generate power when society necessarily needs it; they generate power when the weather dictates.
To compensate for this fundamental mismatch, proponents of 100% renewable grids point to battery storage. Yet, the mathematics of grid-scale storage are devastating. To power a major industrialized region solely on renewables during a multi-day weather anomaly, a prolonged period of low wind and low sunlight, known in energy economics as a “Dunkelflaute” would require a battery infrastructure so massive that it transcends economic reality. The relentless mining of lithium, cobalt, and copper required to build these hypothetical storage networks would not only exhaust national treasuries but also trigger severe supply chain monopolies and new geopolitical conflicts. We are attempting to solve an atmospheric crisis by engineering a mineral one.
One need only look at Europe for a real-world case study of this policy failure. Germany’s ambitious Energiewende (energy transition) involved pouring hundreds of billions of euros into wind and solar infrastructure while simultaneously, and prematurely, shutting down its perfectly functional nuclear fleet. The macroeconomic result has been stark: Germany now faces some of the highest industrial electricity prices in the world. More ironically, to keep the grid stable when renewable generation drops, the country has frequently been forced to fall back on burning lignite coal. This paradox highlights a brutal economic truth: overinvesting in intermittent renewables without a reliable baseload inevitably leads to fossil fuel dependency.
Furthermore, the demand landscape of the global economy is shifting rapidly. We are entering the era of artificial intelligence. The colossal data centers required to train and run AI models operate 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. They cannot function on a power supply that disappears when the sun sets or the wind dies down. The Energy Return on Investment (EROI) of a grid heavily reliant on intermittent renewables backed by vast battery arrays is simply too low to sustain the explosive energy demands of the AI revolution and advanced manufacturing.
If we are serious about achieving decarbonization without triggering deindustrialization, we must abandon outdated ideological dogmas. The green transition desperately requires a nuclear renaissance.
Nuclear power remains the only energy source capable of providing zero-carbon, high-density, dispatchable baseload electricity at scale. For decades, traditional environmental movements have paralyzed nuclear development through fear-mongering rooted in 20th-century paradigms. Today, advanced nuclear technology, particularly Small Modular Reactors (SMRs), offers unparalleled safety, efficiency, and scalability.
Unlike sprawling solar and wind farms that consume massive tracts of land and require the construction of thousands of miles of new, expensive transmission lines, nuclear plants possess an incredibly small geographic footprint. They can plug directly into existing grid infrastructure, providing the raw, uninterrupted power necessary to sustain heavy industry, power water desalination plants, and run the digital economy.
The macroeconomic implications are unavoidable. Nations that stubbornly pursue completely renewable grids will increasingly face grid instability, skyrocketing electricity prices, and industrial flight. In contrast, countries that anchor their clean energy transition with a robust nuclear foundation will secure a profound competitive advantage in the 21st century.
Ultimately, the global energy transition is not a romantic morality play; it is a complex mathematical and macroeconomic challenge. You cannot run an advanced civilization on the unpredictable whims of the weather. It is time to replace green idealism with mathematical pragmatism. Embracing a nuclear renaissance is no longer just an alternative option, it is the fundamental prerequisite for a secure, decarbonized, and prosperous global economy.

articles.full_text:
09/24/2026
In expanding investment by European companies in Korea, not only market size but also regulations, the business environment, and communication between the government and businesses act as important variables. In particular, as industrial structures such as AI and supply chains change rapidly, the areas for cooperation between Korean and European companies are also expanding. 'APK 2026,' a major Asia-Pacific event for the German business community, is scheduled to be held in Seoul this coming October. Against this backdrop, approximately 200 representatives from German and French companies in Korea, as well as officials from the government, diplomatic, and business sectors, gathered to discuss Korea's investment environment and current regulatory issues.
The German Chamber of Commerce in Korea (KGCCI) and the French Chamber of Commerce in Korea (FKCCI) jointly held a special meeting with Prime Minister Han Sung-sook at the Banyan Tree Hotel in Jung-gu, Seoul on the 22nd.
Approximately 200 people attended the event, including business leaders from Europe, such as Germany and France, as well as officials from the government, diplomatic, and economic sectors. The event was organized to expand communication between the Korean government and European companies and to discuss the foreign investment environment as well as regulatory and business challenges faced in the field.
The event began with opening remarks by KGCCI Chairman Park Hyun-nam and FKCCI Chairman David Pierre Jalicon. German Ambassador to Korea Georg Schmidt, French Chargé d'affaires Philomen Robin Pierron, and EU Ambassador to Korea Hugo Astuto attended, and Foreign Investment Ombudsman Kim Doo-sik also discussed Korea's investment environment and measures to promote foreign investment.
Prime Minister Han noted that Korea, Germany, and France are partners who share the values of free trade, a rules-based international order, openness, and innovation, and expressed the government's commitment to cooperating for European companies' investment in Korea. In a congratulatory message released by the Prime Minister's Office, Prime Minister Han also stated that the government would cooperate to ensure that the investments and initiatives of German and French companies translate into tangible results in Korea.
German and Asia-Pacific Business Leaders Gather in Seoul in October… Discussions on Cooperation to Expand to APK 2026
The '19th Asia-Pacific German Business Conference (APK 2026)' to be held in Seoul this coming October was also discussed as a major agenda item at this meeting.
APK 2026 will be held from October 29 to 31 at the Grand Intercontinental Seoul Parnas. According to the German Chamber of Commerce in Korea, approximately 800 business, government, and academic representatives from Germany and the Asia-Pacific region are expected to attend to discuss the global trade order, industrial AI, supply chains, and geopolitical risks.
Prime Minister Han also mentioned APK 2026 at the meeting and said he hoped it would be an opportunity for Korean and German companies to find new investment and cooperation opportunities.
Voices from the corporate field were also heard. Christoph Harmann, CEO of Merck Healthcare Korea, and Han Hyun-soo, CEO of Arkema Korea, participated in the panel discussion to share their views on Korea's investment environment, regulatory improvements, and business challenges.
Park Hyun-nam, Chairman of KGCCI, emphasized that communication between companies and a stable business environment serve as the foundation supporting investment and innovation. He added that he hopes direct exchanges between Korean companies and the German business community will lead to actual business cooperation through APK 2026.
To mark the 140th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Korea and France and the 40th anniversary of the founding of FKCCI, economic and industrial cooperation with France will also be expanded. FKCCI plans to hold a 'Korea-France Symposium' on the theme of innovation and technology at the French National Assembly in Paris on October 16. It will also establish 'Maison France by FKCCI,' an exchange hub combining Chamber of Commerce office space, a business center, a lounge, and a French café, to support connections between companies and investors from both countries.

                        Shri Shripad Naik, the Minister of State for Power and New and Renewable Energy, held a bilateral meeting with a delegation of the European Parliament’s Committee on Industry, Research and Energy (ITRE), in New Delhi, on 24 September 2026. The meeting was held to review and further strengthen the ongoing cooperation between India and the European Union in the power sector.
The discussions covered a wide range of areas, including energy security, power sector transformation, low-carbon development, nuclear energy, carbon markets and development of new technologies. Both sides exchanged views on ongoing initiatives and explored avenues to deepen collaboration, building on the strong momentum in India-EU relations, including the significant progress achieved in the India-EU Free Trade Agreement.
Shri Shripad Naik highlighted India’s rapidly transforming power sector and the country’s efforts to build a resilient, reliable and future-ready energy system. He noted India’s progress in expanding non-fossil fuel capacity, including achieving the NDC commitments in this regard much ahead of the target, strengthening transmission and distribution infrastructure, deploying energy storage and smart-grid solutions, and advancing nuclear energy, energy efficiency and green hydrogen.
Both sides discussed opportunities for enhanced cooperation in emerging areas, including long-duration energy storage, digital power-system technologies, green hydrogen, carbon capture, utilization and storage, and nuclear technologies, including Small Modular Reactors. They also exchanged perspectives on carbon markets and the evolving carbon-pricing landscape, including Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM).
The meeting reaffirmed the importance of energy and power cooperation as a key pillar of the India-EU partnership. Both sides expressed their commitment to continued engagement, exchange of expertise and deeper technological and institutional cooperation to support secure, resilient and sustainable energy systems.

Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
Evonik has rejected a €10.3bn offer from its larger German rival BASF, sparking a potential takeover battle amid a push for mergers in Europe’s struggling chemicals industry.
Ludwigshafen-based BASF recently offered about €22.15 per share as an initial proposal, according to people familiar with the matter. But Evonik said the bid was too low to warrant formal negotiations or to allow its competitor to carry out due diligence, they added.
The bid would mark a nearly 29 per cent premium to Evonik’s share price last Monday before speculation about takeover interest became public. The offer would give Evonik an enterprise value of about €14.2bn, according to Bloomberg data. 
The FT reported last week that BASF had approached Evonik about a possible takeover but details of the price offered have not previously been made public.
The size of the premium may increase pressure on Evonik’s management and its biggest shareholder, the RAG-Stiftung foundation, to justify their unwillingness to engage. Evonik’s shares were trading at €19.29 on Monday afternoon.
Investors in BASF, whose shares fell 3.6 per cent on Friday when the approach became public, are also likely to seek its explanation for pursuing a costly and complex merger that would expand its geographic and product mix.
A potential acquisition of Evonik would “strengthen and complement BASF’s core businesses and we would be disciplined in our approach”, the group said in a statement on Monday, adding that any synergies “can only be validated with the engagement of Evonik”. 
Evonik confirmed last week that it had received a “nonbinding” takeover approach but that “currently there are no talks taking place”. BASF, which has a market value of about €44bn, said at the time it had held “exploratory talks” with the RAG-Stiftung foundation and Evonik, adding that the “course and outcome” of the discussions “remain open at this stage”. 
A takeover would be a bold move by BASF chief executive Markus Kamieth to consolidate Europe’s fragmented chemicals industry and build a company that could better compete with Chinese rivals, including Sinopec, as well as American competitors such as Dow. 
But any tie-up could also lead to job cuts and asset sales to remove overlaps between the two businesses. Shareholders, management and politicians will have to weigh the benefits of building a Germany-based champion with combined revenues of €74bn against the risks of a complex merger and associated cost cuts.
The position of RAG-Stiftung, which has a 44 per cent stake in Evonik, will be key to whether any deal is reached. The foundation was created in 2007 by the German government, states and trade unions to manage the costly phasing-out of the country’s hard coal mining industry.
RAG’s board of trustees includes Hendrik Wüst, premier of North Rhine-Westphalia who is seen as the country’s “chancellor-in-waiting”, German finance minister Lars Klingbeil and Katherina Reiche, the economy minister.
Michael Vassiliadis, head of the IGBCE chemicals and energy union, is also a member of RAG’s board of trustees as well as a supervisory board member at BASF. 
Earlier this year, Vassiliadis called for “concerted consolidation” to support the sector in the long term. He has recused himself from decision-making about the potential takeover, said people familiar with the matter.
But Vassiliadis warned on Monday that a BASF-Evonik combination would not benefit workers and production sites simply by creating a larger company.
He called for commitments on investment and the future of German and European sites. “Both companies should be careful not to turn the screw too far,” he said.
Evonik is run by interim chief executive Claus Rettig, who took over after Christian Kullmann stepped aside in August due to illness. Kullmann predicted in May that the European chemical industry would see significant consolidation.
Germany launched a national strategy in March to help turn around the industry, which faces high energy costs, global overcapacity, weaker demand and rising overseas competition.
Both BASF and Evonik have been restructuring to focus on their core businesses. BASF, which has more than 100,000 employees in more than 90 countries, has been selling peripheral assets and cutting costs and jobs to boost profits. 
Evonik, which operates in more than 100 countries with about 31,000 employees, is cutting jobs, closing plants and selling non-core assets.
Evonik and RAG declined to comment.

ECB FAQs
The European Central Bank (ECB) in Frankfurt, Germany, is the reserve bank for the Eurozone. The ECB sets interest rates and manages monetary policy for the region. The ECB primary mandate is to maintain price stability, which means keeping inflation at around 2%. Its primary tool for achieving this is by raising or lowering interest rates. Relatively high interest rates will usually result in a stronger Euro and vice versa. The ECB Governing Council makes monetary policy decisions at meetings held eight times a year. Decisions are made by heads of the Eurozone national banks and six permanent members, including the President of the ECB, Christine Lagarde.
In extreme situations, the European Central Bank can enact a policy tool called Quantitative Easing. QE is the process by which the ECB prints Euros and uses them to buy assets – usually government or corporate bonds – from banks and other financial institutions. QE usually results in a weaker Euro. QE is a last resort when simply lowering interest rates is unlikely to achieve the objective of price stability. The ECB used it during the Great Financial Crisis in 2009-11, in 2015 when inflation remained stubbornly low, as well as during the covid pandemic.
Quantitative tightening (QT) is the reverse of QE. It is undertaken after QE when an economic recovery is underway and inflation starts rising. Whilst in QE the European Central Bank (ECB) purchases government and corporate bonds from financial institutions to provide them with liquidity, in QT the ECB stops buying more bonds, and stops reinvesting the principal maturing on the bonds it already holds. It is usually positive (or bullish) for the Euro.

articles.title: Semiconductor Chipsets Market Forecast to 2035: Growth Driven by AI and Automotive Demand - IndexBox
articles.summary: Semiconductor Chipsets Market Forecast to 2035: Growth Driven by AI and Automotive Demand  IndexBox
articles.full_text:
Intel
Dominant in PC/server chipsets
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Semiconductor Chipsets market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global semiconductor chipsets market is entering a transformative decade, with demand fundamentals shifting from volume-driven consumer electronics toward performance-intensive, application-specific platforms. Between 2026 and 2035, the market will be shaped by the proliferation of AI inference at the edge, the software-defined vehicle architecture, and the densification of 5G and forthcoming 6G networks. These forces are not merely incremental; they are redefining chipset design priorities, qualification cycles, and supply chain configurations.
The market is bifurcating into high-validation, program-locked OEM supply for automotive and industrial applications, and a more fragmented, service-intensive aftermarket and retrofit ecosystem. Success in each requires divergent operational models. The validation and qualification burden for safety-critical chipsets often exceeds the silicon cost itself, creating a powerful moat for incumbents with established OEM-approved vendor status. Supply chain resilience has superseded pure cost optimization as a primary procurement driver, leading to strategic dual-sourcing mandates and geographic diversification of backend manufacturing.
Pricing power is asymmetrically distributed, concentrated among leading-edge logic and AI accelerator suppliers, while mature-node microcontroller markets face intense competition. This report provides a structured, commercially grounded analysis of the market through 2035, covering demand architecture, supply chain logic, competitive positioning, and regional dynamics.
The baseline scenario for the global semiconductor chipsets market anticipates a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 6.2% from 2026 to 2035, with the market index reaching 182 (2025=100). This outlook assumes a moderate global economic environment, continued semiconductor demand growth in automotive and industrial sectors, and no severe supply chain disruptions. The baseline scenario is supported by the increasing semiconductor content per vehicle, the build-out of AI data centers, and the replacement cycle in consumer electronics. However, the market will not grow uniformly.
Advanced-node chipsets for AI and high-performance computing will see double-digit growth, while mature-node chipsets for simple microcontrollers will face price erosion and intense competition. The automotive segment will be the fastest-growing end-use sector, driven by electrification, ADAS, and infotainment systems. The smartphone segment will remain the largest but will grow slowly, with demand saturated in developed markets and replacement cycles lengthening. Geographically, Asia-Pacific will maintain its dominance in both production and consumption, but North America and Europe will increase their share through fab construction and supply chain localization incentives.
The baseline scenario also assumes that export controls and geopolitical tensions will continue to shape the market, particularly for advanced chipsets, but will not escalate to a full-scale decoupling. Key risks to the baseline include a sharper-than-expected downturn in consumer electronics, accelerated decoupling, and technology disruptions such as quantum computing or neuromorphic chips.
The consumer electronics sector remains the largest end-use market for semiconductor chipsets, encompassing smartphones, tablets, laptops, smart TVs, wearables, and smart home devices. Demand is currently driven by premiumization, with consumers willing to pay more for devices with advanced AI capabilities, better cameras, and longer battery life. However, the overall volume growth is slowing as smartphone penetration saturates in developed markets and replacement cycles lengthen. Through 2035, the sector will see a shift toward AI-enabled devices that require more powerful application processors and dedicated neural processing units. The demand for connectivity chipsets will also grow with the adoption of Wi-Fi 7 and 5G Advanced.
Key demand-side indicators include smartphone shipment volumes, average selling prices, and the attach rate of AI features. The sector is highly competitive, with short design-in cycles and intense price pressure, but also offers high volumes. Major trends include the integration of AI accelerators into smartphones, the rise of foldable and AR/VR devices, and the proliferation of smart home hubs. Companies that can deliver high-performance, energy-efficient chipsets at competitive prices will thrive. Current trend: Moderate growth, driven by premium smartphones and smart home devices.
Major trends: AI integration in smartphones and PCs, Proliferation of smart home and wearable devices, Shift to Wi-Fi 7 and 5G Advanced, Foldable and AR/VR device growth, and Increasing demand for energy-efficient chipsets.
Representative participants: Qualcomm Incorporated, MediaTek Inc, Apple Inc, Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd, Broadcom Inc, and Intel Corporation.
The automotive sector is the fastest-growing end-use market for semiconductor chipsets, driven by the twin forces of electrification and autonomous driving. Modern vehicles are becoming software-defined, with domain and zonal architectures replacing traditional distributed ECUs. This shift requires high-performance chipsets for central compute, as well as a multitude of microcontrollers and sensors for various subsystems. The demand for automotive chipsets is currently characterized by high validation and qualification burdens, with safety-critical applications requiring compliance with ISO 26262 and AEC-Q100 standards.
Through 2035, the semiconductor content per vehicle is expected to increase significantly, particularly for battery electric vehicles (BEVs) and autonomous vehicles. Key demand-side indicators include vehicle production volumes, BEV penetration rates, and the level of autonomy. The sector is also seeing a trend toward vertical integration, with OEMs and Tier-1 suppliers forming strategic partnerships with chipset vendors. Major trends include the adoption of 5nm and 3nm chipsets for central compute, the rise of zonal controllers, and the integration of AI for autonomous driving. Companies with strong automotive-grade portfolios and long-term OEM relationships will benefit. Current trend: Strong growth, driven by electrification and ADAS.
Major trends: Software-defined vehicle architecture, Electrification and battery management, ADAS and autonomous driving, Zonal and domain controllers, and Over-the-air updates and connectivity.
Representative participants: NXP Semiconductors N.V, Infineon Technologies AG, Renesas Electronics Corporation, Texas Instruments Incorporated, Qualcomm Incorporated, and STMicroelectronics N.V.
The industrial and IoT sector encompasses a wide range of applications, including factory automation, robotics, medical devices, energy management, and smart cities. Demand for semiconductor chipsets in this sector is driven by the ongoing digital transformation of industries, which requires reliable, low-power, and secure chipsets for sensing, control, and connectivity. Currently, the sector is characterized by long design-in cycles and a high degree of customization, with customers requiring robust supply chains and long-term support. Through 2035, the growth will be propelled by the adoption of Industry 4.0 technologies, such as industrial IoT, edge computing, and AI-enabled predictive maintenance.
The demand for connectivity chipsets will also rise with the deployment of private 5G networks in factories. Key demand-side indicators include industrial capex, robot installations, and IoT connections. Major trends include the convergence of IT and OT, the rise of edge AI, and the increasing focus on cybersecurity. Companies with a broad portfolio of industrial-grade chipsets and strong ecosystem support will be well-positioned. Current trend: Steady growth, driven by automation and Industry 4.0.
Major trends: Industry 4.0 and smart manufacturing, Edge AI and predictive maintenance, Private 5G networks in factories, Robotics and automation, and Energy efficiency and sustainability.
Representative participants: Texas Instruments Incorporated, Analog Devices, Inc, Infineon Technologies AG, STMicroelectronics N.V, NXP Semiconductors N.V, and Renesas Electronics Corporation.
The data centers and networking sector is experiencing explosive growth, driven by the insatiable demand for AI training and inference, as well as the expansion of cloud services. Semiconductor chipsets for data centers include high-performance CPUs, GPUs, AI accelerators, and networking chips (e.g., SmartNICs, DPUs). Currently, the sector is dominated by a few major players, with NVIDIA leading the AI accelerator market. The demand is characterized by high performance requirements, rapid technology cycles, and significant capital investment. Through 2035, the growth will be sustained by the proliferation of large language models, generative AI, and the build-out of hyperscale data centers.
The demand for networking chipsets will also grow with the transition to 800G and 1.6T Ethernet. Key demand-side indicators include data center capex, AI model sizes, and cloud revenue. Major trends include the adoption of chiplets, the rise of custom AI chips (e.g., Google TPU), and the integration of AI into networking. Companies that can deliver leading-edge performance and energy efficiency will capture the most value. Current trend: Very strong growth, driven by AI and cloud computing.
Major trends: AI training and inference at scale, Cloud computing and hyperscale data centers, 800G and 1.6T Ethernet, Chiplet-based designs, and Custom AI accelerators.

articles.full_text:
The Swedish Migration Agency’s new logo is now being introduced
The Swedish Migration Agency has a new logo, which is now being introduced. The new logo, featuring a heraldic coat of arms, is intended to make it clearer that the Agency is part of the Swedish state.
“With the new logo, we want to make it even clearer that the Swedish Migration Agency is Sweden’s migration authority,” says Eva Carlstedt, Director Communication Department at the Swedish Migration Agency.
The new logo is being introduced gradually across all digital and physical channels. The Swedish Migration Agency’s website is the first to feature the new logo, followed by the Agency’s digital services, letters and decisions, among other channels. The logo on signs and flags, for example, will be replaced at a later stage. On other existing materials, the old logo will be phased out gradually.
As the new logo is being introduced gradually, the Swedish Migration Agency’s old and new logos will appear alongside each other for some time.
“To avoid any uncertainty about whether a communication is from the Swedish Migration Agency, we will clearly communicate that the change is taking place, particularly to our applicants,” says Eva Carlstedt.
How this affects organisations that use the logo
The Swedish Migration Agency’s new logo will be used from 1 September. Organisations that use the Agency’s logo, for example on websites, in systems or in documents, should therefore replace the old logo with the new one.
The new logo is available to download from the Swedish Migration Agency’s website. More information about the rules for using the logo is also available there. The logo is available in both Swedish and English versions.
More about the new logo
The purpose of the Swedish Migration Agency’s new logo, featuring a heraldic coat of arms, is to make it clearer that the Swedish Migration Agency is Sweden’s migration authority and part of the Swedish state. The change also marks a new phase in the Agency’s remit and in its European cooperation following the introduction of the EU’s new common rules on migration and asylum (the Pact on Migration and Asylum).
All Swedish government agencies may use a royal crown and shield as their symbols. These so-called heraldic coats of arms are subject to special protection rules and are clearly associated with public authorities.
